items.title: Annie Ross interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: When I went to Paris. I was living in Paris and Moody, James Moody, had written a tune with no words, which was kind of prophetic in a way, because I’ve sung many songs without words, and it was called “Le Vent Vert” and that was the very first time I ever made a record.

ctx.x: When was your first chance to record?

When I went to Paris. I was living in Paris and Moody, James Moody, had written a tune with no words, which was kind of prophetic in a way, because I’ve sung many songs without words, and it was called “Le Vent Vert” and that was the very first time I ever made a record.
Did you set the words to it?

items.title: Annie Ross — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Klook and Moody had the band. I think it must have been about 10 pieces, or maybe even 12. We were rehearsing in the afternoon.

ctx.x: You were talking about how you were in this club where you used to go down, and there was a piano. Then you talked about your group with James Moody and your arrival in Paris at 17, and the group with . . .

Oh yeah. So, I’m in awe. I was so in awe of Sarah and Billie Holiday. Dinah [Washington], of course, but I didn’t become friends with Dinah until later. Klook and Moody had the band. I think it must have been about 10 pieces, or maybe even 12. We were rehearsing in the afternoon. Klook had gotten hold of the chart of If You Could See Me Now, which I loved. I learned it upside down and backwards. I was sitting there in the afternoon, and Klook said, “Okay, get out If You Could See Me Now.” I thought, oh, good, at…
Let’s go ahead and pause there. Annie, if you could pick it back up with Tadd Dameron.
